"Free-wheeling" paddlewheel: The river currents around Rainier, OR at the time of the casualty
were estimated to be around four knots. The swift-moving waters of the Columbia River were strong
enough to permit the cosmetic paddlewheel to begin turning slowly in a "forward" direction. When
Mr. Staples slipped, witnesses observed him trying to grasp at the wheel for balance. But instead of
finding purchase, the wheel unbalanced him further until he fell into the water. Furthermore, he was
observed traveling under the paddlewheel immediately after entering the river, and he may have
become injured. A simple safety mechanism preventing the wheel from "free-wheeling" in the
current may have permitted him to firmly grasp the unmoving wheel and regain his balance.
Drills and training: According to vessel records, the P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST conducted
thorough and timely drills, including "Man Overboard" drills. Two of the three crewmen in Mr.
Staples' presence at the time of his fall overboard knew exactly what steps to take to ensure the rest

Additionally, none of the crew could recall any training on procedures to take if they are the
individual to fall in the water. Witnesses stated that Mr. Staples appeared to be aware and active, but
made no attempt to call out for help, make a flotation device using his clothing, or to attempt a swim
to shore. Brief discussions with experienced vessel crew during scheduled training sessions about
what to do if a crewmember found him or herself in the water could have been life-saving
information for Mr. Staples.

QUEEN OF THE WEST to carry only three life rings, and three were found onboard, investigators

Instead, the closest life ring was found four decks above at the operating station. By that time, Mr.
Staples had drifted too far to reach with a thrown ring.
